title: India Puts All Maritime Agencies on 'Heightened Alert' After Three Tanker Strikes in Five Days
excerpt: The shipping ministry directive comes as trade unions demand answers, 300,000 Indian seafarers work on vessels worldwide, and New Delhi summons the US diplomat for a second time in three days
body:
India's shipping ministry has directed all government agencies to remain on "heightened alert" and maintain readiness to respond to any contingency involving Indian seafarers or maritime interests, in the strongest official response yet to a week of US military strikes on Indian-crewed tankers.

The directive, issued Thursday, follows three separate US strikes on commercial vessels crewed by Indian sailors in the Gulf of Oman in just five days. Three Indian seafarers were killed on Wednesday when the US Navy fired precision munitions into the engine room of the Palau-flagged M/T Settebello. Twenty Indian crew members had to be rescued from a third tanker, the M/T Jalveer, struck on Thursday night. An earlier strike on the M/T Marivex on Monday had also endangered Indian crew.

## Second Summoning in Three Days

On Friday morning, India summoned the US deputy chief of mission Jason Meeks to the Ministry of External Affairs for the second time in three days — a rare diplomatic escalation between two nations that have spent two decades building a close strategic partnership.

"MEA summoned Meeks to lodge a protest against attacks on commercial vessels off the coast of Oman," an Indian official told Reuters. "Yesterday, yet another vessel with 20 Indian crew on board came under attack."

The first summoning came Wednesday, shortly after the Settebello was struck. India's foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal was blunt: "The attacks that are happening must stop."

The US Embassy in New Delhi did not respond to requests for comment.

## 'Panic and Fear' Among Seafarers

India is one of the world's largest suppliers of merchant marine labour, with more than 300,000 seafarers working on vessels globally, according to the Forward Seamen's Union of India. Many work on foreign-flagged vessels operating in the volatile waters around the Strait of Hormuz, leaving them exposed when tensions escalate.

Manoj Yadav, FSUI's general secretary, said the recent attacks had triggered "panic and fear" among Indian seafarers, many of whom have been stranded in the Gulf since the Iran conflict began in February. He questioned why the US military needed to strike a commercial ship carrying no ammunition when it could "easily board the ship and detain the ship."

The union has denounced the strikes as a "gruesome attack" on "dedicated maritime professionals." The Centre of Indian Trade Unions was sharper: "When a foreign military kills Indian workers in international waters, the government of India must speak — loudly and firmly."

## Families Demand Answers

The father of one of the killed seafarers, Rajesh Sharma, told news agency ANI: "I have only one demand: that my son's remains be brought back. I want to know what happened in his last moments."

Ramji Chaurasiya, the father of another victim, said he had spoken to his son just a day before the attack. "He said everything was alright," Chaurasiya recalled, before breaking down in tears.

India's ports and shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal confirmed that the bodies of all three sailors have been located and will be repatriated. The government, he said, "stands firmly with the bereaved."

## What Comes Next

The Directorate General of Shipping has issued an advisory urging all Indian seafarers on both Indian and foreign-flagged vessels transiting conflict-affected waters to "exercise the highest degree of caution and vigilance."

The crisis arrives at a particularly delicate diplomatic moment. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to meet President Trump on the sidelines of the G7 summit in Évian-les-Bains, France, next week. India's opposition has framed the deaths as a test of Modi's much-vaunted personal rapport with Trump.

"The Prime Minister cannot evade responsibility when that relationship fails to protect Indian lives," the Indian National Congress said in a statement.

The US military says its blockade, in place since April 13, has disabled nine non-compliant vessels, redirected 135 others, and allowed 42 humanitarian aid ships to pass. US Central Command maintains that each struck vessel "repeatedly failed to comply with directions" and was attempting to transport Iranian oil in violation of the blockade.

For India, the calculus is straightforward. Its seafarers cannot become collateral damage in a war between two other nations. The shipping ministry's heightened alert may be the first step. Whether it proves to be the last will depend on what Modi brings back from France.
